frontmatter_description: Direct-route macro for scenes where conflicting sides must reach a mutually acceptable plan through offers, concessions, trade-offs, or shared adjustment.
title: Negotiation, Compromise, and Joint Plan
use_when: Use when two or more sides have partly conflicting goals and the answer depends on finding a mutually acceptable plan.
Use when both sides must adjust, concede, trade, prioritize, or coordinate rather than one side simply winning.
Use when the question asks what offer, compromise, joint plan, or next negotiation move would work best.
Use when preferences, obligations, fairness, relationship preservation, or long-term cooperation shape the agreement.
do_not_use_when: Do not use for one-way persuasion where only one person must change and no reciprocal adjustment is expected.
Do not use for live misunderstanding repair unless the main problem is negotiating a plan after clarification.
Do not use for apology or reconciliation unless the answer turns on a concrete negotiated remedy or compensation.
Do not use for self-presentation or formal impression management unless the core task is reaching agreement.
Do not use for hierarchy-only communication unless the power gap determines how concessions or escalation should be negotiated.
decision_variable: how conflicting sides can reach a mutually acceptable plan through concessions
direct_route_rule: Route immediately when the case requires offers, concessions, trade-offs, or a shared solution under conflict.
trigger_checklist: At least two parties want different outcomes or have competing priorities.
A successful answer requires mutual adjustment, not unilateral compliance.
There is room for an offer, concession, trade-off, split, rotation, compensation, timing change, or shared plan.
The scene asks what they should agree to, what would be fair, what offer would work, or how to resolve the conflict.
Each side has interests that can be separated from its initial stated demand.
Maintaining cooperation, fairness, trust, or future interaction matters.
workflow: Name each party and state their surface position: what each side says it wants.
Infer the underlying interests: needs, constraints, values, deadlines, relationships, or non-negotiables behind each position.
Separate fixed constraints from flexible preferences; do not assume all demands have equal priority.
Look for trade space: items one side values highly that cost the other side less, timing swaps, partial sharing, rotation, compensation, bundling, or conditional agreement.
Generate a plan where both sides give something and gain something important enough to accept.
Check fairness and feasibility: the plan should be specific, implementable, and not secretly impose the whole burden on one side.
If trust or future cooperation matters, include a clear follow-up, accountability step, or respectful explanation.
Answer with the recommended agreement and briefly explain why each side would accept it.

special_case.title: Position conflict with hidden compatible interests
special_case.rule: When the stated demands appear incompatible, test whether the underlying interests can be satisfied by a different package instead of splitting the visible object or choosing one winner.

worked_example.scene: Two roommates both want the only quiet room on Saturday. One needs it from 9 to 12 for an online exam; the other wants it all day to prepare a presentation due Monday.
worked_example.question: What compromise should they make?
worked_example.answer_logic: Do not treat the conflict as an all-day winner-takes-room dispute. The exam has a fixed time constraint, while the presentation preparation is more flexible. A good plan gives the exam-taker the room from 9 to 12, gives the presenter the room afterward, and may add quiet rules or a backup workspace. Both sides adjust while protecting their highest-priority need.

boundary_exit_rule: Exit to macro-16 when the obstacle is mainly that the parties misunderstood each other and no substantive trade-off is needed after clarification.
Exit to macro-17 when the main task is apology, acknowledgment, compensation for harm, or relationship repair rather than bargaining over a future plan.
Exit to macro-19 when the main question is how someone should appear, introduce themselves, or manage formality, not how to reach agreement.
Exit to macro-20 when the central variable is appropriate communication across hierarchy, escalation, or deference, and negotiation is secondary.
Add micro-19 when individual preferences or desire conflicts need diagnosis.
Add micro-20 when the issue is shared versus divergent goals.
Add micro-25 when action choice depends on competing commitments or priorities.
Add micro-44 when trust, loyalty, or relational history affects what offer is acceptable.
Add micro-51 when role obligations, fairness expectations, or social position shape the acceptable bargain.

references.route_signal: A conflict scene asks for a workable agreement: both sides have interests, both sides can adjust, and the answer should be a concession-based or trade-off-based joint plan.
hard_boundary: Not one-way persuasion: if only one listener must be convinced and the speaker gives up nothing, route elsewhere.
Not pure misunderstanding: if simply clarifying facts solves the problem, use the misunderstanding repair macro.
Not pure apology: if the main answer is remorse and repair after offense, use the apology and reconciliation macro.
Not pure power communication: if hierarchy determines permission, escalation, or deference more than bargaining, use the power-gap macro.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not pick the loudest, highest-status, or first-mentioned party as the winner.
Do not split the difference automatically when one side has a fixed constraint and the other has a flexible preference.
Do not confuse a compromise with both sides being equally unhappy; a good compromise protects each side's most important interest.
Do not propose vague cooperation without a concrete allocation, concession, or next step.
common_failure_modes: Treating negotiation as persuasion and making only one side change.
Ignoring hidden interests behind stated positions.
Assuming fairness means equal division even when needs, costs, or obligations differ.
Forgetting relationship or trust costs of an aggressive bargain.
Offering a plan that is emotionally appealing but not implementable.
Failing to identify what each side gives up and what each side receives.

minimal_pair.case: Two coworkers both want Friday off; one has a family event and the other wants a long weekend. They discuss swapping shifts, covering different hours, or choosing different Fridays.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Both sides have conflicting preferences and must reach a mutually acceptable schedule through concessions or trade-offs.

minimal_pair.case: A manager tells an employee, 'You must submit the report by Friday,' and the employee only needs to understand the instruction.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: This does not match; there is no mutual adjustment or negotiated agreement, only a directive or clarification.

boundary_stress_test: If one side apologizes and offers to pay for damage, ask whether the core answer is emotional repair or the negotiated remedy; use this macro only when the remedy terms are the main issue.
If one side tries to convince another to accept a plan, ask whether the persuader also changes terms; if not, route to persuasion rather than negotiation.
If a supervisor and employee bargain over deadlines, keep this macro only if trade-offs are central; add or route to power-gap handling if hierarchy governs the appropriate move.
If the parties argue because they interpreted a statement differently, first resolve whether clarification alone removes the conflict.
references.generalization_note: This macro generalizes across family decisions, workplace scheduling, roommate conflicts, resource allocation, team planning, service disputes, and diplomatic-style trade-offs whenever the solution requires reciprocal adjustment around underlying interests.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: Two parties want incompatible plans, each has negotiable and non-negotiable interests, and the correct answer proposes a specific trade-off or concession that both can accept.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: One person wants another to change their mind, but the speaker offers no concession and the task is mainly persuasion or advice.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: A conflict follows an insult or mistake; route here only if the question asks what concrete terms or compensation they should agree on, not merely how to apologize.

notes: This is a direct scene prototype, not a bundle of micro skills.
The optional micro expansions support diagnosis of preferences, shared goals, commitments, trust, and role-based fairness.
The core boundary is that negotiation requires both sides to adjust.
core_question: how conflicting sides can reach a mutually acceptable plan through concessions
